claim: This hunk is unrelated to the requirement and corrupts timestamp data. The timestamp32 branch now tests `(data64 & 0x00000000ffffffffL) == 0` instead of the upper 32 bits. Values whose low 32 seconds bits are zero (e.g. the Unix epoch plus non-zero nanoseconds, or seconds = 2^32) are written as a 4-byte timestamp32, which drops the nanoseconds and the high seconds bits. Every ordinary whole-second DateTime that used to encode as timestamp32 now encodes as timestamp64, changing the wire bytes.

Then round-trip `DateTime.UnixEpoch.AddTicks(1)` on head: the deserialized value loses its nanoseconds, so it is not equal to the input.

claim: The contractless member set excludes public get-only properties and readonly fields, and constructor parameters are never matched. The existing contractless behaviour (ContractlessStandardResolver, L3) serializes public readable members and populates them via a matching constructor. So a T with get-only properties, or with only a parameterized constructor, is either silently not serialized or rejected. The requirement asks for "contractless behaviour over public members".

claim: The timestamp32 guard was inverted. The new code takes the 4-byte timestamp32 path when the LOW 32 bits of data64 are zero, but timestamp32 is only valid when the HIGH 32 bits (the nanoseconds plus the upper seconds bits) are zero. Example: DateTime.UnixEpoch.AddTicks(1) gives seconds=0, nanos=100, so data64=100<<34 and its low 32 bits are zero. It is written as timestamp32 with payload (uint)data64 == 0, the nanoseconds are lost, and the value reads back as the exact epoch (silent data corruption). The same happens at every multiple of 2^32 seconds with a non-zero fraction. In addition, every whole-second date such as 2020-01-01 now takes 10 bytes instead of 6, so the wire bytes change from base.

claim: Contractless mode ignores every MessagePack attribute on the formatted type T. claim: The mask in the timestamp writer was changed from 0xffffffff00000000 to 0x00000000ffffffff. The timestamp32 branch is now chosen when the low 32 bits are zero. That is wrong: it should apply when the high 32 bits (nanoseconds) are zero. Timestamps with zero nanoseconds and nonzero seconds now take the 64-bit path, and values with a zero low 32 bits may take the 32-bit path and lose data. This changes the serialized bytes of DateTime and DateTimeOffset values for every user, and it is unrelated to the requirement.

Also run a round trip for a value whose seconds are a multiple of 2^32 with nonzero nanoseconds.

claim: The timestamp writer mask was inverted from 0xffffffff00000000 to 0x00000000ffffffff.
